slides.title: Introduction How to increase the power of an engine ?
slides.body:
How to increase the power of an engine?
- Increase the displacement
(larger cylinders or more
cylinders)
- Increase the maximum engine
speed
- Increase the maximum torque by increasing in-cylinder maximum pressure

slides.title: Turbocharging
slides.body:
o Goal: More air, more oxygen, more fuel can be burned, more power can be obtained
o Practically: use a compressor that increases the pressure in the intake manifold
The compressor is mechanically connected on the
same axis to a turbine that converts the waste
energy in the exhaust gases (hot and at relatively high
pressure) into mechanical power.
The mechanical power to move the compressor
comes (almost) for free!
The turbine and compressor assembly form the so
called turbocharger

slides.title: Pros&Cons
slides.body:
o In a SI, indirect injection engine, the main objective and advantage is to increase the torque, thus power using a smaller engine.
o The presence of the compressor that ‘’pushes’’ the air into the engine, reduces the overall pumping losses (it’s the compressor that
pushes the air into the cylinder and not the piston that has to ‘’suck’’ the air in). This is true only if the compressor is ‘’pumping’’ enough
(medium-high load depending on the turbocharger).
o In a diesel engine peak power and overall efficiency are ALWAYSincreased, just because i am using energy that would otherwise
be wasted.
o This is true also for a SI engine without direct injection if the engine and turbocharger are matched in order that the best effciency of
the turbocharger (on the BFSC chart) is HIGH where the engine efficiency is low.
PROS
o The overall system complexity (hence cost) is increased.
o The turbocharger introduces a series of degrees of freedom in the system that have to be controlled in order to guarantee best effciency and
integrity.
o The air compressed by the compressor may need to be cooled through and INTERCOOLER, otherwise the cycle low temperature raises
and efficiency decreases.
o Turbine and compressor inertia may introduce a delay in the system known as turbo-lag.
CONS

slides.title: Turbocharging Wastegate&Variable Geometry Turbine (VGT)
slides.body:
The wastegate (WG) valve bypasses a fraction of the hot exhausts into the exhaust line without letting it pass into the turbine.
The wastegate valve opening is controlled by the ECM in order to limit turbine speed (the turbine revs up to 250.000rpm)
and/or boost pressure and thus the air mass pumped to the intake by the compressor.
In order to do so, ECM uses information from the EBP (exhaust boost pressure) and MAP (manifold absolute
pressure) sensor
The variable geometry turbine (VGT) can modify the flow
conditions by adjusting the vanes through an electronic
(actuator controlled by ECM) or hydraulic mechanism (engine
oil, valves managed by ECM).
When the vanes are opened, the effect is the same as the
wastegate (that is no longer required).
This solution allows to optimize the compressor boost pressure
along the whole rpm and torque range.
This solution gives more control on the airflow and supports
control policies to reduce pollutants emission.
The VGT strongly mitigates or eliminates turbo lag.

slides.title: Exhaust Gas Recirculation valve EGR Overview
slides.body:
EGROverview
The EGR valve (controlled by the ECM), recirculates a fraction of the exhaust gases towards
the intake.
The exhaust gases are inert in the combustion chamber. As a consequence, this reduces
the in-chamber temperature, reducing the NOx production.
The NOx production also decreases because of the reduced oxygen availability.
With accurate engine design and calibration the soot that is recirculated in the EGR flow can
be burned (smaller particles) or can be increased in size (good for the pollution, bad for the
engine).
Large soot particles can be trapped more easily in the DPF but increase fouling of the
exhaust lines, intake manifold, EGR valve, EGR cooler etc.
EGR flow needs to be cooled down before being forwarded to the intake
manifold, this is done through a dedicated heat exchanger: the EGR
cooler

slides.title: GDI
slides.body:
GDI
- Dishomogeneous charge (stratified) at low loads: stoichometric (or slightly rich) mixture
(AFR=AFRst) nearby the spark plug in order to start combustion, lean to very lean mixture
(AFR>>AFRst) away from the spark plug.
- Higher compression ratios can be achieved.
- The throttle is still present but can be kept fully open during stratified charge operation.
- At medium/high loads the ECM normally switches to homogeneous charge mode (AFR=AFRst
everywhere, similarly to port injection).
- In-chamber fluid dynamics requires accurate design in order to obtain the desired fuel
concentration in stratified charge mode and adequate air-fuel mixing in homogeneous charge
mode.
- Often, a traditional port injector is installed for homogeneous charge operation.
- Critical combustion control during transients (normally switches to homogeneous). Limited
advantages in case of conventional powertrains, but more potential in case of hybrid powertrains.
- Increased system complexity.
- More sophisticated fuel injectors.
- Due to limited time for air-fuel mixing, soot formation can occur.
- Due to lean combustion conditions, higher NOx emissions.

slides.title: Variable Valve Lift and Timing (VVL - VVT)
slides.body:
Variable Valve Lift and Timing (VVL-VVT)
- An hydraulic , electrical or mechanical system can be adopted to vary the valve lift.
- With variable valve lift, the intake air flow can be regulated through the intake valve/s, potentially
allowing the elimination of the throttle body (reduction of the pumping losses).
- Variable valve timing allows to optimize the opening and closing time of the valves, allowing a better
filling of the cylinder (exploitation of dynamic effects in the manifold).
- VVT allows to obtain a more favourable torque profile (improved torque at both high and low rpm)
that would not be possible with a fixed cam timing.
- Some degree of «inner EGR» can be achieved by acting on the valve timing (exhaust gases can be
sucked back into the cylinder) without using an EGR loop.
- The pumping losses can be reduced by anticipating intake valve closing and exhaust valve opening.
- Almost all manufacturers have their proprietary VVL/VVT systems, often associated with other
systems aimed at increasing engine efficiency and/or performance (BMW Valvetronic, Porsche:
Variocam, FCA: Multiair, Honda:VTEC…).
- There are systems with continuously variable valve timing (Valvetronic, top image) and finite
variable valve timing (Honda VTEC- 2 timings).

slides.title: FCA Multiair
slides.body:
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Td9Gz_h7Qpg
The camshaft 2 is the same for the intake and exhaust valves.
The exhaust valves are directly actuated by the traditional cammes.
The cam 2 acts on the hydraulic pump 4 (works like a syringe) through the rocker 3.
The intake valves are actuated by the hydraulic pistons 6 that receive the pressurized oil
from the pump 4 through the electronically controlled electrovalve 5.
The actuation of the intake valves is decoupled from the camshaft motion.
The system is hydraulic and uses the engine oil as operating fluid.

slides.title: Catalytic converter Exhaust aftertreatment systems
slides.body:
- A first catalyst is used to oxidize the incomplete combustion
products (CO+HC). This catalyst operates correctly in stoichometric
to lean mixture conditions. This is used in both SI and Diesel
engines.
- In Diesel engines, the system is denominated DOC (Diesel
Oxidized Catalyst) and operates at a temperature above 200°C.
- In SI engines, the catalyst is Platinum/Palladium based and has
an operating temperature above 600-700°C.
- A second Rhodium Based catalyst is used to reduce the nitrogen
oxides. This catalyst operates in rich to stoichometric conditions. It
cannot be used in Diesel engines for their excess air operation.
- In order to obtain the best conversion efficiency for all pollutants, the
mixture shall be approximately stoichometric (lambda sond).
In order to monitor the catalyst operation and diagnose faults/degradation, the lambda sond is duplicated.
The two lambda sonds are installed uphill and downhill the catalyst.
As long as the two lambda sonds detect different oxygen concentrations, the catalyst is operating correctly.
When the two concentration are too similar, catalyst degradation/fault is detected.

slides.title: Exhaust aftertreatment systems DPF/GPF
slides.body:
- The system is basically constituted by a metal or ceramic matrix that mechanically captures the
soot particles.
- The metal matrix may be loaded or constituted by a catalytic element that lowers the temperature
when the oxidation process starts.
- During operation, especially in traffic driving conditions (low load, high EGR, low exhaust
temperature), the carbon particles build up inside the filter.
- The pressure drop across the DPF increases progressively as the soot deposits build up. The
pressure drop is measured by a differential pressure sensor.
- When the pressure drop increases above a certain threshold, the ECM actuates the DPF
regeneration strategy:
- Fuel post injection (depending on current load conditions) in order to increase exhaust
temperature (Tex>450-500°C).
- Dedicated low-EGR strategy (increase oxygen availability at the exhaust)
DPF
GPF
- The system is similar to DPF.
- Soot formation is relevant for direct injected (GDI) SI engines only.
- The pressure drop across GPF is monitored to trigger GPF regeneration.
- In SI engines, the exhaust temperature is higher, so no additional fuel has to be burned to raise the exhaust temperature.
- GDI – SI engines operate with less oxygen excess respect to Diesel engines. GPF regeneration is executed during cut-offs (deceleration)
and/or by increasing airflow (through throttle or VVL) and reducing spark advance (in order to prevent knock).

slides.title: Exhaust aftertreatment systems SCR ( Selective Catalytic Reduction )
slides.body:
SCR (Selective Catalytic Reduction)
- An aqueous solution of urea (AdBlue) is injected uphill a dedicated
reactor.
- The urea decomposes to form ammonia, that is the actual reactant.
- Ammonia is flammable, toxic and volatile, that’s the reason why
urea (safe) is used instead.
- The reactor is made of multiple channels where the exhaust-
ammonia current mixes up and NOx reduction by means of a
Vanadium-based catalyst (selective) takes place.
- The ammonia reduces the NOx so that Nitrogen and Oxygen are the
results of the reaction.
- Nitrous oxide concentration is very low in the exhaust gases (1%) so the
dwelling time of the exhaust-ammonia current in the catalyst shall be long
enough to assure good conversion efficiency.
- The more ammonia, the higher the NOx reduction rate.
- Increasing the amount of ammonia increases the ammonia that slips to the
exhaust (to be avoided).
- For this reason, the SCR has a second stage ASC (Ammonia slip catalyst)
that has the ability to absorb excess ammonia (slipped from the first stage)
and use it when the amount of NOx produced increases (works as an
ammonia buffer) and the conversion into the first stage is insufficient.
